en: From those dogs, our ancient enemies,
To suffer this humiliation
Once again, it seems we came.
My darling orphan,
Have you seen what I have seen?
A deep-dug pit comes toward us,
A teeming, countless army comes,
Haze comes, fire comes,
Bullets that strike unerring come!
Mighty Abyke and Kobosh come.
Led by the forty warriors, my orphan,
An army worth the whole world comes.
The damned ones bring a threat to life!
If seven wolves tear at one yearling,
Will they leave its carcass?
If so many enemies beat one lone child,
Will they leave his body?
The one horse as precious as life itself—
Is a young child now to ride him?
Creator, I entrust him to You alone!
Grant a better time to his head.
Only Creator, what can I do?
Keep my only son safe!
My saintlike peers,
Give support to my only son,
My lions gone to the world beyond!
Syrgak and Serek, twin heroes,
Almambet and Chubak, heroes equal to them,
God, set his affairs right!
You four, joining together,
My orphan goes forth—give him aid!
My Talas, whose protector lives,
Who attacked countless Chinese,
My saintlike Manas,
My orphan goes forth—watch over him!
Forty chiltens, my Khizr Niyaz,
Be companions to the orphan!’
Your two mothers stood side by side,
Raising their hands and crying aloud.
Spreading their palms and saying, ‘Amen,’
They gave their blessing, sobbing.
Taking his mother's blessing,
The orphan now mounted,
With the painted spear left by his father Khan Manas,
In the broad ravine where no bird flew,
Mounted upon the noble steed Buurul,
He rode tall to confront
His kinsmen Abyke and Kobosh.
What remedy is there? Hard is the task,
When Allah Most High has ordained it.
Speaking his sorrow, Semetey
Stood crying out again,
To his kinsmen Abyke and Kobosh.
Sitting tall upon Buurul,
Your orphan turned his horse,
And stood in his full stature.
He was no mountain of yellow ridges;
There was no cause to fight him,
Nor was he an enemy come from China.
‘If I am the one you would contend with,
Here are the Kyrgyz people with their sovereign.
If brutishness should overtake you,
Here I am, if you would cut off my head!
Buurul is my offering, my head is my offering.
Do not dig my pit deep.
Attacking worse than the Kalmyks,
Do not boil up my misery!
We share one root, one nest.
Restrain your accursed army,
And gather in your anger!
I will offer my mother Kanykei;
Six elder kinsmen, I will wed her to one of you!
In Temir Khan's city,
Wandering, I grew up.
Now that the orphan has returned,
Do not have them call him unruly.
My dear elder kinsmen,
Do not bring a curse upon us!’
Before he could close his mouth,
Khan Manas's forty warriors
Drew bows in a rain of arrows,
And fired bullets like hail.
With shrill shouts and ringing battle cries,
Abyke's army formed a separate body,
Shouting ‘Gray-Maned One!’ as their battle cry,
Kobosh's army formed a separate body.
Bearing pale-mottled flags and banners,
Raising a clamorous uproar,
As though to destroy him altogether,
As though to overwhelm him completely.
They drove forward in a mass,
Spreading over the swaying earth.
The commanders of ten bobbed about.
Their renowned men were at the front,
Their champions upon the flanks.
Their lancers separated,
Their hostile intent was plain.
Once they themselves attacked,
Would the leopard merely watch?
The offspring of the blood-drinker—
Would God strike him down for standing idle?
‘Your father's grave, my six elder kinsmen!
Let the guilt be on your own heads,
Your suffering upon your own dark crowns!
Until the swaying stalks ripen,
Until the autumn gossamer flies,
If I torment you thoroughly for six months—
I offer my head, but you will not accept;
You will not cease your massed assault.
I offer my mother, but you will not accept;
You will not cease your redoubled assault!
You have set out to dig pits.
That the gray-maned hero was truly gray-maned
Became plain to the mighty army.
He had spared them as his kin,
But his kin did not spare him.
When he grew wrathful,
The nine who protected him
Took the boy by the hand.
A dark-spotted leopard
Raged at his side,
A short-tailed, gray-maned lion
Made ready before his face.
At one glance, Semetey
Appeared to be one man.
At another glance, Semetey
Appeared to be a thousand men.
His father, Lord Manas—
Of the gray-maned son born surpassing him,
Which deeds shall we tell?
A leopard of chilling might,
Those who looked upon him marveled.
How could those who opposed him remain unharmed?
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A rascal as great as Mount Opol.
When he thrust forward,
He had the form of a dragon.
Looking closely at his back,
He had the majesty of a thousand men.
Anyone who clashed with him would not prosper;
Anyone who attacked him would not go unscathed.
The horse Buurul, as great as a camel,
Was prepared for holy war.
If an enemy came out to fight,
He drove them before him.
When his anger rose,
He caught them in his jaws and chewed them.
No mortal went to face him;
None who faced him remained alive.
As they came face to face,
Let me tell you of the champion.
Seeing his unmistakable form,
The Kyrgyz people grew deeply troubled.
‘How can we attack the champion?’
The dear people stood unwilling.
‘How did we come to attack the gray-maned hero?’
The dear people stood dispirited.
For the Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
He had found their remedy,
He had shattered and driven
All the unwilling people.
‘Against the blood-drinker's orphan son,
With what face have we raised our hands?’ they said.
Ashamed, the people swayed,
Shifting as though about to flee.
As troops for Abyke,
Many people had come under compulsion.
The gray-maned hero's orphan son
They had examined closely.
For the gray-maned hero's orphan son,
They were dying with longing.
‘Your father's grave, this world!
If not for Abyke and Kobosh,
If we gathered together in unity,
And raised this one as khan,
The Russians on the right
He is a son who could crush for us.
Against China beyond the hills,
He is a servant who could bring slaughter.
His father, gray-maned Manas—
This one is born surpassing him!
Our making war upon the boy
Is God's punishment upon us!
When leopard Manas died,
Abyke and Kobosh rose as khans.
Their might drove souls out.
If we do not obey the villains,
If we do not join this army,
“Give sixty camel-loads of tea,
Give six thousand fat yearlings,” they demand.
They torment and humiliate us.
Our means of escape are exhausted.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six villains—
How can we live under their wrath?
Against the blood-drinker's orphan son,
With what face can we raise our hands?’
The great multitude came creeping,
Whispering to one another,
Without the power to speak aloud.
The oppression of the six villains—
Driving them out and onward
Was Abyke and Kobosh's force.
The mighty army shouted ‘Gray-Maned One,’
And raised ‘Kobosh!’ as its battle cry.
Do not ask about the six villains.
They had no livestock left to drive away,
Nor the heart to turn back from Semetey.
The forty warriors and the six villains
Were the formidable ones in that great army.
Along the banks of broad Talas,
They came spreading out.
At the army's front, the forty warriors,
Wielding their battle-axes,
Drove it forward.
Among the Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
They came forward with difficulty.
The gray-maned one among all the villains,
The fool Kobosh, their elder, cried:
‘Drive the army, drive it!
This orphan of Manas—
Troops, surround and bind him!
Bind both his hands,
Gouge out both his eyes,
Drag him onto the road,
And tear him apart for the great hounds!
Take vengeance in this way!’
When Kobosh gave the command,
Could the multitude merely stand and watch?
Covering the earth with their numbers,
The great army charged and attacked.
One escorting another under guard,
Earth flew up, dust covered everything,
Like flying tumbleweed.
One could not tell who was who.
God, do not let us see their faces!
One could not tell who was who!
Gray-mottled banners, red standards,
A tumult of cries and shouts!
All around the orphan
Arrows rattled from the bows,
Shots fell thick as hail.
The forty companions left by Manas
Surged shouting through the royal camp,
The points of their spears clashing.
With wild cries they charged,
The warriors racing one another.
The great army came sweeping on,
Closing upon Semetey.
The young lord Semetey
Struck his noble steed upon the flank,
And plunged among the countless troops,
Semetey attacking in earnest.
When Semetey struck,
Those whose appointed time had come died.
They thrust in utter confusion,
Fighting like dogs,
